topics.title: A Series broadcasts down every column
topics.body: A Series lines up with a column axis when you subtract it from a frame, so a per-row vector can be applied to every row without a loop.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
row = pd.Series({"a": 10, "b": 20})
print(df.add(row, axis="columns").values.tolist())

topics.title: where builds a conditional column
topics.body: `where` is a vectorised if: keep the value where the condition holds and substitute otherwise. It is the safe way to add a status column without apply.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"marks": [40, 75]})
df["band"] = df["marks"].where(df["marks"] >= 50, "fail")
print(df["band"].tolist())

topics.title: cumsum builds a running column
topics.body: A cumulative sum keeps one value per row, so revenue can be charted against a target without a second aggregation.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"sales": [10, 20, 5]})
df["running"] = df["sales"].cumsum()
print(df["running"].tolist())

topics.title: round, floor and ceil are three rules
topics.body: `round` goes to the nearest value, `floor` always down, `ceil` always up. Billing and capacity planning need different ones, and pandas exposes both numeric and `.dt` versions.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1.4, 2.5])
print(s.round().tolist(), s.apply(lambda v: int(v)).tolist())

interview.q: What is the difference between `assign` and plain column assignment?
interview.answer: `assign` returns a new frame and can be chained inside a pipeline, so the input stays untouched. `df["x"] = ...` mutates the frame in place, which is fine in a script but makes a long chain hard to test.

interview.q: Why does a percentage column produce inf, and how do you prevent it?
interview.answer: Division by zero yields inf (or a warning), and inf then poisons means and charts. Replace zero denominators with NaN before dividing, then decide explicitly whether to fill, drop or flag those rows.

topics.title: sort_values decides where NaN goes
topics.body: `na_position` puts missing values first or last. The default is last, which is why a sorted column can hide its gaps at the bottom.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([3.0, None, 1.0])
print(s.sort_values(na_position="first").tolist())

topics.title: rank can be a percentage
topics.body: `rank(pct=True)` returns the position as a share of the rows, which is how a column becomes a percentile score without a second step.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40])
print(s.rank(pct=True).round(2).tolist())

topics.title: corrwith compares two frames column by column
topics.body: `corrwith` pairs columns by name and returns one correlation per pair, which is the quickest way to see which features move with a target column.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

a = pd.DataFrame({"x": [1, 2, 3], "y": [3, 2, 1]})
b = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])
print(a.corrwith(b).round(2).to_dict())

topics.title: quantile uses 0 to 1
topics.body: `quantile(0.25)` and `percentile(25)` ask the same question on different scales. Mixing them puts the median at 0.5 or 50 by accident.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(s.quantile(0.5))
print(s.quantile([0.25, 0.75]).tolist())

interview.q: How do you explain a mean that is far above the median?
interview.answer: A long right tail: a few very large values pull the mean up while the median stays at the typical observation. Report both, inspect the top values, and choose the statistic the decision needs.

interview.q: Why is correlation not enough to claim a relationship?
interview.answer: It measures linear co-movement only, can be produced by a third variable or a shared trend, and is sensitive to outliers. Plot the pair and check the relationship inside segments before reporting it.

topics.title: isna().any(axis=1) finds incomplete rows
topics.body: Reducing the missing mask along the columns answers "which rows have at least one gap", which is the count a data-quality note needs.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [1, None], "b": [None, 2]})
print(df.isna().any(axis=1).tolist())
print(df.isna().all(axis=1).tolist())

topics.title: fillna takes a different rule per column
topics.body: A dict fills each column with its own value, so text and numbers do not share one default that is wrong for both.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"score": [10.0, None], "city": [None, "Pune"]})
print(df.fillna({"score": 0.0, "city": "unknown"}).values.tolist())

topics.title: dropna how decides the rule
topics.body: `how="any"` drops a row with any gap, `how="all"` only when every value is missing. The default is aggressive, so name it.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"a": [None, 1], "b": [None, None]})
print(df.dropna(how="all").shape[0])
print(df.dropna(how="any").shape[0])

topics.title: interpolate can limit the fill distance
topics.body: `limit` and `limit_direction` stop interpolation from bridging a long gap, which keeps an isolated missing point from becoming invented data.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([0.0, None, None, 30.0])
print(s.interpolate(limit=1).tolist())

interview.q: How do you report handling missing data honestly?
interview.answer: State how many values were missing in each affected column, which rule was applied, and what it changes — an imputed mean reduces variance, and dropping rows changes the population. A reader must be able to see which rows the number came from.

interview.q: Why is `ffill` dangerous on a measurement column?
interview.answer: It asserts the value did not change, which is true for a status and false for a measurement. On a temperature column it creates a plateau and understates the variation, so the statistic describes the fill rule more than the data.

topics.title: duplicated keep=False marks every copy
topics.body: The default marks all but the first copy; `keep=False` marks every row involved, which is what you need to see a whole duplicate pair.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1, 2]})
print(df.duplicated().tolist())
print(df.duplicated(keep=False).tolist())

topics.title: rename can change the index too
topics.body: `rename(index=...)` relabels rows and `rename(columns=...)` relabels columns. Both return a new object unless `inplace=True`.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"v": [1, 2]}, index=["r1", "r2"])
out = df.rename(index={"r1": "first"})
print(out.index.tolist())

topics.title: A z-score flags distance in std units
topics.body: The z-score divides the deviation by the standard deviation. It is comparable across columns, unlike a raw threshold, but it assumes a roughly normal spread.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([10, 12, 11, 40])
z = (s - s.mean()) / s.std()
print(s[z.abs() > 1.5].tolist())

topics.title: replace accepts a regex
topics.body: `replace({"r": {"^-$": ""}}, regex=True)` turns a sentinel into an empty value across a table, which is how an export's placeholders become real missing data.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"city": ["-", "Pune"]})
out = df.replace({"city": {r"^-": ""}}, regex=True)
print(out["city"].tolist())

interview.q: What makes a cleaning step reviewable?
interview.answer: A count before and after, the rule that was applied, and why. "Removed duplicates" is not reviewable; "removed 412 rows where id repeated, keeping the newest by updated_at" is.

interview.q: Why prefer IQR over a fixed threshold for outliers?
interview.answer: The IQR adapts to the column's own spread and ignores the tail when computing the bounds, so one extreme value cannot widen the threshold enough to hide itself. A fixed threshold requires knowing the domain.

topics.title: zfill pads numeric-looking ids
topics.body: `str.zfill` pads to a fixed width, which makes ids sort and join consistently instead of mixing 7 and 0007.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series([7, 42]).astype(str)
print(s.str.zfill(4).tolist())

topics.title: str.cat joins two text columns
topics.body: `str.cat` concatenates columns with a separator and handles missing values, replacing the string `+` that fails on NaN.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"first": ["Aman"], "last": ["Sharma"]})
print(df["first"].str.cat(df["last"], sep=" ").tolist())

topics.title: str.slice takes positions
topics.body: `str.slice(0, 2)` takes characters by position, which is the quickest read of a fixed-width code such as a state prefix.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["MH-PUN-01", "DL-DEL-02"])
print(s.str.slice(0, 2).tolist())

topics.title: str.get reads one piece of a split
topics.body: `str.split(...).str.get(1)` extracts one element without expanding the column, so the frame shape stays the same.
topics.code:
import pandas as pd

s = pd.Series(["pune|MH", "delhi|DL"])
print(s.str.split("|").str.get(1).tolist())

interview.q: When do you stop using `.str` and parse instead?
interview.answer: When the text is a serialised structure — JSON, HTML, a nested field. Regex over it is unreadable and breaks on the first nesting; use the parser that owns the format, then hand the fields to Pandas.

interview.q: Why normalise case and whitespace before a join on text?
interview.answer: Joins compare exactly, so "Pune" and "pune " never match and the join silently drops rows. Normalising both sides first makes the match reflect the data rather than the formatting.
